newsitem.title: USA: WORLD BONDS - U.S. T-bonds almost ripe for picking.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - U.S. T-bonds almost ripe for picking.

text.p: While convergence trades may not offer the same rich returns next year that investors reaped in 1996, European bond plays are still a better bet than U.S. Treasury securities in the near term, global strategists said.

However, international bond specialists are keeping close tabs on the U.S. Treasury market, waiting for signs of slower U.S. economic growth, perhaps in the first quarter, to shift out of Europe into U.S. instruments.

Ed Vaimberg, managing director of asset management at Bear Stearns and Co Inc, said the United States stands out for not being a dog. But while he is looking for opportunities to sell Europe to overweight the U.S. bond market, the timing is not yet right.

It would be premature to underweight the higher-yielding European markets relative to U.S., Vaimberg said. "Simply because those countries continue to be in the process of cutting rates in an environment of subdued economic growth and respectable fiscal restraint."

Progress towards European economic and monetary union (EMU), combined with tepid overseas economic growth in 1996, made offshore fixed-income markets more attractive than the United States, where the economy expanded at a respectable 2.1 percent yearly rate in the third quarter, on the back of frothy 4.7 percent growth in the second.

The U.S. bond market has seesawed in recent weeks, leading some global investors to seek a safer posture in shorter maturities, especially those of overseas markets where bonds may also soon be buffeted by strengthening economies.

"I think the bull market is over," said Michael Rosenberg, head of international fixed-income research at Merrill Lynch & Co Inc. "The data are coming in stronger of late, and investors have been overweight bonds and they have taken real rates too low.
"The U.S. may be more vulnerable than Germany and Japan, but overall it's a general defensive posture you want to take," he added.

After reaching a low of about 6.35 percent in November, the 30-year U.S. Treasury bond yield rose to 6.70 percent on Wednesday and then closed at less than 6.60 percent Thursday, the lowest in about a week.

"Sometime early in the year, when it looks like first-quarter growth will be slower than fourth quarter, then the U.S. will probably offer somewhat better relative value," said Richard Koss, international strategist at MFR Inc. "You are talking about yield in the long end around 6.75 (percent), somewhere in that neighborhood."

Investors said the themes in the global bond market at the outset of 1997 should remain the same as this year's. But rather than hitting home runs, playing the spread-narrowing game in Europe, investors may have to settle for base hits.
"Yields are going to be looking a lot more similar across the board," Koss said. "I mean that is what convergence is. So it's much harder to take on a buy-and-hold strategy."

For instance, the yields of 10-year German and Italian government bonds converged dramatically in 1996. Investors discounted Italy's re-entry to Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) as well as EMU, taking advantage of one of the widest differentials in the European Union.

But Italy's membership in ERM is no guarantee of it joining the single currency, and investors see much less scope in 1997 for 10-year differentials between Germany and Italy to narrow very much from the current 175 basis points.
"Italy is the one where it seems to me the risks are actually a little bit more on the other side than Spain and Sweden and some of these places," said MFR's Koss.
"I have a modest bet in favor of convergence; I currently have it in favor of Sweden more than anything else," Vaimberg of Bear Stearns added.
